etymology: From American slang grungy, dirty or shabby (recorded by the mid-1960s, perhaps a blend of grubby and dingy); back-formed as grunge, filth. As a name for music it is usually credited to Mark Arm of the Seattle band Green River (later Mudhoney), who used it of his own sound in the early 1980s, and it was taken up by Seattle’s Sub Pop label in the late 1980s. The style went national with Nirvana’s Nevermind (September 1991) and "Smells Like Teen Spirit," alongside Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, and Alice in Chains. The word also named the look: thrift-store flannel, ripped jeans, unwashed hair, and studied indifference.
biblical_def: Grunge was the sound of Gen X shrugging: sludgy guitars, mumbled lyrics, flannel from the thrift store, and a mood somewhere between boredom and despair. Its anthem ended in a chant of "a denial," and its brightest star, Kurt Cobain, took his own life in April 1994. A father should speak of that with grief, not contempt; a great many young people heard in grunge the first honest admission that the suburbs and the shopping mall had not filled them. The Christian observation is that the Bible got there first. The Preacher tried pleasure, work, and wealth and concluded, "all is vanity and vexation of spirit" (Ecc 1:14). The Psalmist interrogated his own gloom: "Why art thou cast down, O my soul?" — and then commanded it, "hope thou in God" (Psa 42:5). Grunge stopped at the diagnosis; Scripture goes on to the cure. Christ calls exactly the weary, flannel-clad generation that grunge described: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mat 11:28). He came not to numb a life but to fill it: "that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly" (Joh 10:10). He gives "the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness" (Isa 61:3). A father can tell his son: the ache those songs named is real, and it is not the end of the story — there is a Man who carries the heavy laden, and He does not shrug.
webster_summary: Gen X name (Seattle, late 1980s; national with Nirvana’s Nevermind, 1991) for sludgy, despairing rock and its flannel-and-indifference look; Scripture shares the diagnosis — all is vanity (Ecc 1:14) — and supplies the cure, rest in Christ (Mat 11:28).
webster_full: GRUNGE, n. and adj. (Gen X slang, late 1980s–1990s, Seattle) A style of rock music marked by heavy, distorted guitars and bleak, mumbled lyrics; also the unkempt fashion that went with it. "He traded the letter jacket for grunge flannel."
From grungy (US slang, 1960s), dirty, shabby; grunge rock, grunge look, grunge band; centered on Seattle’s Sub Pop label.
Icons: Nirvana, Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, Alice in Chains; thrift-store flannel, ripped jeans, combat boots, long unwashed hair.
No entry in Webster 1828; the word is a 20th-century American back-formation from grungy.
Decode for parents: grunge named a real emptiness honestly; meet the ache with the gospel, not with a lecture about haircuts.
scriptures: Ecc 1:14
I have seen all the works that are done under the sun; and, behold, all is vanity and vexation of spirit.
Psa 42:5
Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.
Isa 61:3

To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that he might be glorified.
corruption_summary: Grunge told the truth about the emptiness of a prosperous, fatherless age and then made a home in the emptiness; Scripture names the same vanity and calls the heavy laden to Christ for rest.
corruption_paragraphs: Despair as a style. Grunge began as honesty and hardened into a pose: the slouch, the mumble, the refusal to care, sold back to teenagers by the same record companies the music scorned. Apathy became fashionable, and fashionable despair is still despair. The Psalmist shows a better way to be honest about gloom: he names it, then argues with it — "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? … hope thou in God" (Psa 42:5). Sorrow that talks to God is godly; sorrow that only talks to itself goes down into the dark.

The diagnosis without the cure. Ecclesiastes is the Bible’s grunge album: all is vanity under the sun (Ecc 1:14). But the Preacher ends by pointing above the sun, and the gospel finishes the thought. Christ came that men might have life more abundantly (Joh 10:10), and He gives the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness (Isa 61:3). A generation that learned to name its ache needs to hear that the ache has an answer, and that the answer has a name.
roots_summary: US slang grungy (1960s, dirty) → grunge → Seattle’s Green River and Sub Pop (1980s) → Nirvana’s Nevermind (1991) → flannel fashion; Scripture: vanity under the sun (Ecc 1:14), rest in Christ (Mat 11:28).
roots_lines: US slang grungy (mid-1960s) — dirty, shabby, run-down
Back-formation grunge — filth, grime
Early-to-late 1980s Seattle: Green River, Mudhoney, the Sub Pop label
1991 Nirvana’s Nevermind carries the sound and the flannel nationwide
Biblical answer: hope thou in God (Psa 42:5); rest for the heavy laden (Mat 11:28)
usage: "Mom, it’s not dirty, it’s grunge." — c. 1992.
All is vanity and vexation of spirit (Ecc 1:14) — grunge said it second.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden (Mat 11:28).

etymology: From the hardcore punk scene of the early 1980s, where crowds in front of the stage slammed into one another (slam dancing, Los Angeles and Washington, D.C., c. 1980–81). Mosh is commonly traced to D.C., where Bad Brains’ singer H.R. is said to have urged crowds to "mash," the word drifting in pronunciation to mosh; the exact first use is uncertain. Mosh pit, the churning space before the stage, was established in punk and thrash-metal circles by the mid-to-late 1980s and went mainstream with Nirvana-era rock and the Lollapalooza tours of the early 1990s.
biblical_def: A mosh pit is the open floor in front of a punk or metal stage where fans slam, shove, and spin into one another in a kind of violent, sweaty dance. To parents it looked like a riot; to the kids inside it was release, belonging, and noise you could feel in your ribs. One unwritten rule of the pit was honorable: if someone goes down, you pick him up. The Christian observation begins there. The Preacher said the same thing three thousand years earlier: "if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth" (Ecc 4:10). The church is meant to be the place where the fallen are lifted, where we "Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ" (Gal 6:2). But the pit itself trains a young man to treat bodies, his own and others’, as things to be thrown, and to mistake chaos for freedom. "It is an honour for a man to cease from strife" (Pro 20:3), and God’s worship is ordered, not frenzied: "Let all things be done decently and in order" (1Co 14:40). The deepest picture is the word pit itself, which in Scripture is the place of death and helplessness — and the Psalmist sings of the God who "brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock" (Psa 40:2). A father can tell his son: keep the rule that lifts the fallen, and leave the pit; Christ came down into the real one to bring you up.
webster_summary: Hardcore-punk term (early 1980s) for the slam-dancing crowd before the stage; its one good rule — lift the fallen — is Scripture’s (Ecc 4:10), and the Bible’s own pit is the one Christ lifts us out of (Psa 40:2).
webster_full: MOSH PIT, n. (Gen X slang, early-to-mid 1980s, US hardcore punk) The area in front of a stage where fans slam, shove, and jump into one another to loud music. "He came out of the mosh pit with a split lip and a grin."
Mosh, v., to dance so; moshing, mosher; earlier slam dancing, slamming; later circle pit, wall of death.
Pit etiquette: pick up anyone who falls; stage diving and crowd surfing grew up beside it.
Webster 1828: PIT, v.t. To indent; to press into hollows. 1. To mark with little hollows, as by variolous pustules; as the face pitted by the small pocks. 2. To set in competition, as in combat.
Decode for parents: the pit is mostly release and belonging, but it trains a boy to treat bodies as projectiles; honor the rule that lifts the fallen.
scriptures: Ecc 4:10
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.
Gal 6:2
Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
Pro 20:3
It is an honour for a man to cease from strife: but every fool will be meddling.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Psa 40:2
He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings.
corruption_summary: The mosh pit sells controlled violence as freedom and noise as belonging; Scripture honors the one good rule of the pit — lift the fallen — and names the real pit Christ draws us out of.
corruption_paragraphs: Chaos as release. The pit offered teenage boys something the culture had stopped giving them: physical struggle, shared risk, and a place to spend anger. But it offered it without purpose or order. Strife for its own sake is the fool’s pastime (Pro 20:3), and a body thrown around for the thrill is not being honored as the temple of the Holy Ghost. God gives young men real battles — work, defense of the weak, the fight of faith — and asks that even zeal be done decently and in order (1Co 14:40).

The rule worth keeping. Every pit had its code: if someone falls, you stop and pull him up. That instinct is straight out of Ecclesiastes 4:10, and it is a seed of the law of Christ (Gal 6:2). The church should be the place where it is practiced without the bruises. And the word pit should send a son to Psalm 40, where the Lord bends down to a man stuck in the miry clay and sets his feet upon a rock.
roots_summary: Old English pytt → pit → early-1980s hardcore slam dancing → D.C. mash / mosh → mosh pit (mid-1980s) → Lollapalooza mainstream; Scripture: up out of the horrible pit (Psa 40:2).
roots_lines: Old English pytt, from Latin puteus — a well, a hole in the ground
c. 1980–81 Los Angeles and D.C. hardcore: slam dancing
D.C. hardcore: mash heard as mosh (commonly traced to Bad Brains)
Mid-to-late 1980s: mosh pit in punk and thrash; early 1990s Lollapalooza takes it mainstream
Biblical pit: the miry clay, and the God who lifts out of it (Psa 40:2)
usage: "I lost a shoe in the mosh pit and never found it."
If they fall, the one will lift up his fellow (Ecc 4:10) — the pit’s best rule is older than punk.
He brought me up also out of an horrible pit (Psa 40:2).

etymology: Rock slang from the 1970s, origin uncertain, for a heavy-metal fan who whips his head up and down in time with the music (headbanging); it is often traced to the front rows of early heavy-rock tours around 1970. The word became a badge of identity in the 1980s through MTV’s weekly metal show Headbangers Ball (1987–95), and every Gen Xer remembers the car scene to Queen’s "Bohemian Rhapsody" in Wayne’s World (1992).
biblical_def: A headbanger is a fan of heavy metal, named for the motion: head down, hair flying, neck snapping to the beat. In the 1980s the word was both an insult from outsiders and a proud self-label from inside the scene. The Christian observation is gentle here, because the word itself is mostly comic. Scripture is not afraid of loud music or of bodies that move to it: "Praise him upon the loud cymbals: praise him upon the high sounding cymbals" (Psa 150:5). David danced before the LORD with all his might. The question is never volume but direction — what the head is bowing to. In the Bible the head is the seat of honor and the sign of authority. The Psalmist says of God, "thou, O LORD, art a shield for me; my glory, and the lifter up of mine head" (Psa 3:3). The gates are told, "Lift up your heads… and the King of glory shall come in" (Psa 24:7). And over every head stands one Head: Christ, "the head of the body, the church… that in all things he might have the preeminence" (Col 1:18). Music that throws the head about can be play; music that fills the head with darkness is something else, and the line runs through the lyrics, not the amplifier. Paul gives the better soundtrack: "singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord" (Eph 5:19). A father can laugh with his son at the air guitar and still ask him, kindly: who is the head your head bows to?
webster_summary: Gen X / 1970s–80s rock slang for a heavy-metal fan who bangs his head to the beat (MTV’s Headbangers Ball, 1987–95); Scripture welcomes loud cymbals (Psa 150:5) and asks only who is Head (Col 1:18).
webster_full: HEADBANGER, n. (Gen X slang, 1970s–80s, US and UK rock) A fan of heavy metal, especially one who jerks his head violently in time with the music. "The back of the bus was all headbangers."
Headbang, v.; headbanging; often paired with metalhead, air guitar, the devil-horns hand sign.
MTV’s Headbangers Ball (1987–95) made the word an identity; Wayne’s World (1992) made it a family joke.
No entry in Webster 1828; the compound is 20th-century rock slang.
Decode for parents: the word is mostly comic; listen to what is in the headphones rather than what the neck is doing.
scriptures: Praise him upon the loud cymbals: praise him upon the high sounding cymbals.
Psa 3:3
But thou, O LORD, art a shield for me; my glory, and the lifter up of mine head.
Psa 24:7
Lift up your heads, O ye gates; and be ye lift up, ye everlasting doors; and the King of glory shall come in.
Col 1:18
And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.
Eph 5:19
Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
corruption_summary: The headbanger’s fault is not volume but direction; Scripture welcomes the loud cymbal and asks what the head is bowing to, and under which Head.
corruption_paragraphs: Loudness is not the problem. Parents in the 1980s often fought the wrong battle, objecting to noise and hair while ignoring words. The Psalter calls for loud and high sounding cymbals (Psa 150:5); God is not offended by decibels. What He weighs is what a song puts into the mind and where it points the heart. A boy who bangs his head to a song about courage is in a different place from one who bangs it to songs about death and despair.

The head and the Head. In Scripture the head is honor and authority. God is the lifter up of the believer’s head (Psa 3:3), and Christ is the Head of the church, preeminent in all things (Col 1:18). A culture that reduces the head to a thing to be thrown about has lost the sense of what it is for. Teach a son to lift up his head to the King of glory (Psa 24:7), and the rest of his music will start to sort itself out.
roots_summary: Old English heafod (head) + bang → 1970s rock headbanging → 1980s identity label (Headbangers Ball, 1987) → Wayne’s World (1992); Scripture: Christ the Head (Col 1:18).
roots_lines: Old English heafod — head; Norse-derived bang — to strike noisily
c. 1970s hard-rock audiences: headbanging to the beat
1980s heavy metal: headbanger as insult and badge
1987–95 MTV’s Headbangers Ball; 1992 Wayne’s World car scene
Biblical head: the lifter up of mine head (Psa 3:3); Christ the Head (Col 1:18)
usage: "Turn it up! Total headbanger song."
Praise him upon the loud cymbals (Psa 150:5) — the volume was never the issue.
Lift up your heads (Psa 24:7) — the King of glory is the one worth looking up to.

etymology: From heavy metal, a music label drawn from the phrase "heavy metal thunder" in Steppenwolf’s "Born to Be Wild" (1968) and fixed by early-1970s rock critics for the sound of Black Sabbath (1970) and their kin; + -head, devotee (as in older pothead). Metalhead for a committed fan is established by the early-to-mid 1980s, the era of the New Wave of British Heavy Metal (Iron Maiden, Judas Priest), Metallica’s Master of Puppets (1986), and the 1985 Senate hearings prompted by the Parents Music Resource Center that led to the "Parental Advisory" label.
biblical_def: A metalhead is a devoted fan of heavy metal: black band T-shirts, denim jacket covered in patches, long hair, and a record collection that frightened his mother. The 1980s fought loudly over him. Congress held hearings in 1985; parents found occult album covers and lyrics about death; some bands courted the outrage on purpose. Others, it should be said, sang about war, injustice, and addiction with real moral seriousness, and a surprising number of metalheads were quiet, loyal, bookish boys. The Christian observation starts with the root. Scripture is full of metal, and nearly always as a picture of testing and strength. "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend" (Pro 27:17). God is the refiner: "he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver" (Mal 3:3); "thou hast tried us, as silver is tried" (Psa 66:10). Metal is worth having only when the dross is burned out. So it is with what a young man takes into his mind. Paul gives the filter: "whatsoever things are true… honest… just… pure… lovely… think on these things" (Php 4:8). And where the music crosses into the dark arts, the line is plain: "have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them" (Eph 5:11). A father need not burn the denim jacket. He can be the iron that sharpens his son, listen with him, and help him tell the songs that forge a man from the songs that corrode one.
webster_summary: Gen X label (early 1980s) for a devoted heavy-metal fan; Scripture loves the image of metal tried in the fire (Mal 3:3) and iron sharpening iron (Pro 27:17), and tells the young to have no fellowship with works of darkness (Eph 5:11).
webster_full: METALHEAD, n. (Gen X slang, early 1980s, US and UK) A devoted fan of heavy-metal music. "The metalheads hung out by the smoking wall in their Iron Maiden shirts."
From heavy metal (late 1960s–early 1970s) + -head, devotee; also headbanger, metal fan; later subgenres thrash, speed, death, hair metal.
The 1985 PMRC Senate hearings put metal lyrics before Congress and produced the "Parental Advisory" sticker.

Webster 1828: METAL, n. met’l. [Latin metallum.] A simple, fixed, shining, opake body or substance, insoluble in water, fusible by heat, a good conductor of heat and electricity, capable when in the state of an oxyd, of uniting with acids and forming with them metallic salts. …
Decode for parents: do not judge the jacket; read the lyrics, and be the iron that sharpens your son.
scriptures: Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
Mal 3:3
And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the LORD an offering in righteousness.
For thou, O God, hast proved us: thou hast tried us, as silver is tried.
Php 4:8

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
Eph 5:11
And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.
corruption_summary: Metal culture ranges from honest anger at real evil to open flirtation with the occult; Scripture keeps the strong image of metal tried in the fire and draws a hard line at the works of darkness.
corruption_paragraphs: Shock as marketing. Some bands of the 1980s discovered that skulls, pentagrams, and blasphemy sold records to boys looking for something to frighten their parents with. Much of it was theater, but theater about the devil is not harmless play; it teaches a young mind to find darkness glamorous. Scripture’s word is not panic but separation: have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness (Eph 5:11). A father who names the line clearly does more good than one who shouts at the volume.

The metal worth keeping. Strength, endurance, loyalty to friends, and anger at injustice drew many boys to metal, and those are not bad instincts. The Bible honors them and gives them a forge: iron sharpening iron (Pro 27:17), silver tried in the fire (Psa 66:10), the Refiner sitting patiently over His people (Mal 3:3). The cure for a metalhead is not softness; it is a harder, truer metal — a man made strong by God’s fire rather than by noise.
roots_summary: Greek metallon (mine) → English metal → "heavy metal thunder" (1968) → heavy-metal music (early 1970s) → metalhead (1980s); Scripture: iron sharpeneth iron (Pro 27:17), silver refined (Mal 3:3).
roots_lines: Greek metallon — mine, quarry; Latin metallum — metal
1968 Steppenwolf, "Born to Be Wild": "heavy metal thunder"
Early 1970s: heavy metal names the Black Sabbath sound
1980s: metalhead; NWOBHM, Metallica, the 1985 PMRC hearings
Biblical metal: tried as silver (Psa 66:10); the Refiner’s fire (Mal 3:3)
usage: "He’s a metalhead, but he’s the nicest kid in homeroom."
Iron sharpeneth iron (Pro 27:17) — a father’s best answer to a metalhead son.
Whatsoever things are pure… think on these things (Php 4:8).

etymology: From skate (Dutch schaats) + -er; as the name of a youth subculture it means a skateboarder. Skateboarding began among California surfers in the late 1950s and 1960s; its Gen X form was born in the Santa Monica and Venice "Dogtown" of the mid-1970s, where the Zephyr team (the Z-Boys) rode drained backyard swimming pools during the 1976–77 drought. Thrasher magazine (San Francisco, 1981) gave the scene its motto, "Skate and Destroy," and Powell Peralta’s Bones Brigade (Tony Hawk, Steve Caballero, Rodney Mullen) and its videos (from 1984) gave it heroes. Skater style: Vans, baggy shorts, a board under the arm, a punk tape in the Walkman.
biblical_def: A skater in Gen X speech was more than a boy with a skateboard; he was a member of a tribe, with its own magazines, music, shoes, and contempt for "No Skateboarding" signs. The scene had a defiant edge ("Skate and Destroy"), a love of empty lots and drained pools, and a deep loyalty among friends. The Christian observation is that most of what made a skater is good. Skating is hard; it is learned only by falling, hundreds of times, and getting back up. Scripture honors that pattern: "a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again" (Pro 24:16), and the believer who stumbles "shall not be utterly cast down: for the LORD upholdeth him with his hand" (Psa 37:24). The Preacher would approve the skater’s focus: "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might" (Ecc 9:10). Where the culture needs examining is its attitude toward authority and property. The "Skateboarding is not a crime" bumper sticker was clever, but grinding a church handrail after the sign says no is not innocence. "Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers" (Rom 13:1). And the skill, wonderful as it is, has a ceiling: "bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things" (1Ti 4:8). A father can stand at the skate park and cheer every fall-and-rise, then tell his son: you already know how to get up after a fall; learn to do it before God, and learn to respect the sign.
webster_summary: Gen X name (mid-1970s Dogtown, Thrasher 1981) for a skateboarder and his tribe; Scripture honors the fall-and-rise of the skater (Pro 24:16) and asks him to respect the sign as well (Rom 13:1).
webster_full: SKATER, n. (Gen X slang, mid-1970s–1990s, Southern California) A skateboarder, especially one who belongs to the skateboarding subculture with its music, dress, and attitude. "The skaters took over the bank parking lot every Sunday."
Also skate rat, sk8r; Dogtown, Z-Boys, Bones Brigade; tricks: ollie, kickflip, grind, rail slide.
Badges: Thrasher magazine (from 1981, "Skate and Destroy"), Vans sneakers, punk and hip-hop soundtracks, "Skateboarding is not a crime."
Webster 1828: SKATE, n. A sort or shoe furnished with a smooth iron for sliding on ice.
Decode for parents: the skater has learned perseverance by falling; teach him to apply it to the soul and to honor the property line.
scriptures: For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief.
Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down: for the LORD upholdeth him with his hand.
Ecc 9:10
Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.
corruption_summary: Skater culture prizes the good discipline of falling and rising but can wear contempt for authority and property as a badge; Scripture keeps the perseverance and corrects the contempt.
corruption_paragraphs: "Skate and Destroy." The scene’s motto was half joke, half creed. Trespassing in empty pools, grinding the bank’s ledges, and dodging security guards became part of the identity, and the outlaw thrill was much of the fun. But a property owner’s sign and a policeman’s word are not enemies of freedom; the powers that be are ordained of God (Rom 13:1). A Christian skater can ride with everything he has and still go where he is welcome.

The best thing a skater knows. No one lands a trick without falling on it a hundred times. That is the most biblical lesson in the whole subculture: the just man falls seven times and rises up again (Pro 24:16), and the LORD upholds the one who falls (Psa 37:24). Bodily skill profits a little (1Ti 4:8); the same grit turned toward repentance, prayer, and obedience profits for this life and the next. A father who has watched his son bleed for a kickflip already knows the boy can endure; he only needs to show him the race worth enduring for.
roots_summary: Dutch schaats → English skate → 1960s sidewalk surfing → mid-1970s Dogtown Z-Boys → Thrasher (1981) and the Bones Brigade → Gen X skater tribe; Scripture: falleth seven times, and riseth up again (Pro 24:16).
roots_lines: Dutch schaats — skate; English skate (17th c.), ice skate
Late 1950s–1960s California: skateboarding as "sidewalk surfing"
Mid-1970s Santa Monica and Venice: Dogtown, the Zephyr team, pool riding in the 1976–77 drought
1981 Thrasher; 1984 onward Bones Brigade videos; skater names the tribe
Biblical perseverance: the just man riseth up again (Pro 24:16); the LORD upholdeth (Psa 37:24)
usage: "Skaters aren’t allowed at the mall anymore." — c. 1988.
A just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again (Pro 24:16) — every skater already knows the first half.
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers (Rom 13:1), even the one who posted the sign.

etymology: From prep school, short for preparatory school (Latin praeparare, to make ready beforehand); preppie for a prep-school pupil is recorded in the early 1900s, and Ali MacGraw’s Jenny taunts Ryan O’Neal’s Oliver as "Preppie" in Love Story (1970). The word became a national fashion and a Gen X social category with The Official Preppy Handbook (1980, edited by Lisa Birnbach), a tongue-in-cheek guide that turned the Northeastern upper-class look into a mall uniform: Izod Lacoste alligator shirts with popped collars, khakis, madras, Sperry Top-Siders, Polo Ralph Lauren, pearls, and monogrammed sweaters.
biblical_def: In Gen X high schools the preppy was the kid in the pastel polo with the collar turned up, the khakis, the boat shoes, and the expectation of a good college. The look was borrowed from old Northeastern money, and the word carried a social message: we are the ones headed somewhere. To the punks and burnouts, preppy meant snob. The Christian observation is that God sees past both the alligator and the sneer. "Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart" (1Sa 16:7). James knew the preppy problem in the church of his day, where the man "that weareth the gay clothing" was given the good seat and the poor man told to stand (Jas 2:3). "The rich and poor meet together: the LORD is the maker of them all" (Pro 22:2). And yet the root word is a good one. Preppy comes from preparatory, a school that makes a young man ready. Scripture is full of that kind of readiness: the Christian’s feet are "shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace" (Eph 6:15), and every believer is to "be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you" (1Pe 3:15). A father can teach his children to dress neatly and aim high without despising anyone, and to care far more for being prepared for eternity than for looking prepared for Yale.
webster_summary: Gen X social label and fashion (from prep school; The Official Preppy Handbook, 1980) for the polo-and-khakis upper-middle-class look; Scripture forbids respect of persons (Jas 2:3) but prizes the readiness the word once meant (1Pe 3:15).
webster_full: PREPPY, n. and adj. (Gen X slang, 1980s, from US Northeastern prep schools) A student or former student of a private preparatory school; anyone who dresses and behaves in that clean-cut, affluent manner. "She went totally preppy after summer camp."
Also preppie, prep; uniform: popped polo collar, khakis, madras, Top-Siders, pearls, the Izod alligator.
The Official Preppy Handbook (1980) turned a class marker into a mall trend; Love Story (1970) gave the nickname an earlier sting.

Webster 1828: PREPARATORY, a. 1. Previously necessary; useful or qualifying; preparing the way for any thing by previous measures of adaptation. The practice of virtue and piety is preparatory to the happiness of heaven. 2. Introductory; previous; antecedent and adapted to what follows.
Decode for parents: the clothes are harmless; the class pride is not. Teach your children to be ready without looking down.
scriptures: But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
Jas 2:3
And ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing, and say unto him, Sit thou here in a good place; and say to the poor, Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool:
Pro 22:2
The rich and poor meet together: the LORD is the maker of them all.
Eph 6:15
And your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace;
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
corruption_summary: Preppy turned a school’s purpose — making the young ready — into a costume of class; Scripture forbids the respect of persons and keeps the readiness for the gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: Class as costume. The preppy look sold the appearance of old money to anyone with a mall credit card, and with it a quiet message: some people belong in the good seats. James calls that respect of persons and puts it under judgment (Jas 2:3). The opposite sin, the burnout’s sneer at the preppy, is the same pride wearing a different shirt. The LORD is the maker of rich and poor alike (Pro 22:2), and He looks on the heart (1Sa 16:7).

Preparation worth the name. The prep school promised to make a boy ready for Harvard; the gospel makes a man ready for God. Paul arms the believer’s feet with "the preparation of the gospel of peace" (Eph 6:15), and Peter tells every Christian to be ready always to give a reason for his hope (1Pe 3:15). That is a preparatory education no handbook can sell, and it is open to the boy in the thrift-store flannel as much as to the boy in the alligator shirt.
roots_summary: Latin praeparare (to make ready) → preparatory school → preppie (early 1900s) → Love Story (1970) → The Official Preppy Handbook (1980); Scripture: the preparation of the gospel of peace (Eph 6:15).
roots_lines: Latin praeparare — to make ready beforehand
English preparatory school; prep school — private school readying pupils for college
Early 1900s preppie — a prep-school pupil; 1970 Love Story "Preppie"
1980 The Official Preppy Handbook; the popped-collar 1980s
Biblical readiness: feet shod with preparation (Eph 6:15); ready always to answer (1Pe 3:15)
usage: "Nice popped collar, preppy."
Ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing (Jas 2:3) — the oldest preppy problem.
Be ready always to give an answer (1Pe 3:15) — the preparation that counts.

etymology: Ultimately from the Goths, the Germanic people who sacked Rome in 410; Renaissance writers used Gothic to mean barbarous and medieval, and Horace Walpole’s The Castle of Otranto (1764) began the Gothic novel of ruins, ghosts, and dread. The music press applied gothic to dark post-punk at the end of the 1970s; Bauhaus’s "Bela Lugosi’s Dead" (1979) is commonly called the first goth record, with Siouxsie and the Banshees, The Cure, and the Sisters of Mercy following, and London’s Batcave club (1982) gathering the scene. By the mid-1980s goth named both the music and its people: black clothes, pale faces, dark lipstick, silver crosses and ankhs, and a fascination with death.
biblical_def: A goth in a Gen X high school dressed in black from boots to eyeliner, listened to brooding post-punk, read vampire novels, and wore an air of graceful sadness. Many goths were gentle, artistic, lonely kids who found in the darkness a place where their melancholy was taken seriously. The Christian observation must be honest in two directions. First, the church should not sneer at sorrow; Scripture gives whole psalms to it, and the Christian walks "through the valley of the shadow of death" without pretending it is not there — but adds, "I will fear no evil: for thou art with me" (Psa 23:4). Second, the scene’s romance with death and the occult was not always costume. Some of its imagery was borrowed straight from practices God forbids by name: there shall not be found among you "any one that… useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch" (Deu 18:10). Fascination with death is, at bottom, a fear of death dressed in velvet, and Christ came to "deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage" (Heb 2:15). The goth is right that the world is dark; he is wrong that the dark has the last word. "The light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not" (Joh 1:5). And because of the empty tomb the believer can say what no gothic poet could: "O death, where is thy sting?" (1Co 15:55). A father can sit with a daughter in black, take her sadness seriously, and gently show her a Savior who has been to the grave and come back.
webster_summary: Gen X subculture (post-punk, Bauhaus 1979; London’s Batcave 1982) of black dress, dark music, and fascination with death; Scripture takes sorrow seriously (Psa 23:4), forbids the occult (Deu 18:10), and announces the death of death (1Co 15:55).
webster_full: GOTH, n. and adj. (Gen X slang, early 1980s, UK, then US) A devotee of gothic rock and its style: black clothing, pale makeup, dark lipstick, Victorian and occult ornament, and a melancholy, death-haunted mood. "The goths ate lunch on the steps of the auditorium."
Gothic rock, goth rock; baby bat (a young goth), deathrock (the US cousin); icons: Bauhaus, Siouxsie and the Banshees, The Cure, the Sisters of Mercy.
From the Goths of history, through Renaissance Gothic (barbarous, medieval) and the Gothic novel (1764 onward).
Webster 1828: GOTHIC, a. Pertaining to the Goths; as gothic customs; gothic architecture; gothic barbarity. 1. Rude; ancient. 2. Barbarous.
Decode for parents: much of goth is sorrow looking for a home; meet the sorrow with compassion and draw a plain line at the occult.
scriptures: Psa 23:4
Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.
There shall not be found among you any one that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch,
Heb 2:15
And deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage.
Joh 1:5
And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.
O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?
corruption_summary: Goth culture honors sorrow but romances death and borrows the occult’s imagery; Scripture walks through the valley without fear, forbids the dark arts, and proclaims the light that darkness cannot overcome.
corruption_paragraphs: Death made beautiful. The gothic imagination dresses mortality in lace and candlelight until the grave seems elegant. But death is the last enemy, not a muse. The fear of it holds men in bondage all their lifetime (Heb 2:15), and a style that keeps a young person gazing at the tomb can feed that bondage rather than relieve it. Some in the scene went further, from ankhs and vampire lore into tarot, séances, and spells; God names those practices and forbids them (Deu 18:10), and a father must too.

Sorrow that needs a home. Yet the goth often saw something the bright suburb missed: that the world is broken and grief is real. Scripture agrees, and gives the grieving a better companion than the dark. The believer walks through the valley of the shadow of death with the Shepherd beside him (Psa 23:4). The light shines in darkness and is not overcome (Joh 1:5). The gospel does not ask the sad to pretend; it shows them a risen Christ and lets them say, "O death, where is thy sting?" (1Co 15:55).
roots_summary: The Goths (Germanic tribe) → Renaissance Gothic (barbarous) → the Gothic novel (1764) → post-punk "gothic rock" (Bauhaus, 1979) → Gen X goth; Scripture: the light shineth in darkness (Joh 1:5).
roots_lines: Late Latin Gothi — the Goths, who sacked Rome in 410
Renaissance Gothic — barbarous, medieval; later the pointed-arch architecture
1764 Walpole’s The Castle of Otranto begins the Gothic novel of ruin and dread
1979 Bauhaus, "Bela Lugosi’s Dead"; 1982 the Batcave, London; goth names the scene
Biblical answer: no fear in the valley (Psa 23:4); death’s sting removed (1Co 15:55)
usage: "She went goth over the summer — black everything."
Though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil (Psa 23:4).
The light shineth in darkness (Joh 1:5) — the line the goth never got to sing.

etymology: An old English word of uncertain origin with a disreputable history: in Shakespeare’s day a punk was a harlot; by the early 20th century American slang used it for a worthless young man, a petty hoodlum, or a coward ("to punk out," to back down), the sense Clint Eastwood made famous in Dirty Harry (1971). American rock critics of the early 1970s applied punk rock to raw 1960s garage bands; then Punk magazine (New York, 1976), the Ramones’ first album (1976), the club CBGB, and in London the Sex Pistols’ "Anarchy in the U.K." (1976) and "God Save the Queen" (1977) fixed it as the name of a loud, fast, defiant music and its look: safety pins, torn shirts, spiked or Mohawk hair, and a do-it-yourself ethic.
biblical_def: Punk had two meanings for Gen X. The older one was an insult: a punk was a young hood, a loudmouth, or a coward who talks tough and then runs. The newer one was a badge: a punk was a kid who played three-chord songs as fast as possible, cut his own hair, made his own records, and sneered at the system. The movement’s slogans were anarchy and "no future," and some of its early records mocked the crown and the church on purpose. The Christian observation is that the Bible has seen anarchy before and does not admire it: "In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Jdg 21:25). Proverbs describes a whole "generation that curseth their father, and doth not bless their mother" (Pro 30:11), and Samuel warned a king that "rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft" (1Sa 15:23). But punk also smelled something true: that the respectable world was often hollow, that conformity is not the same as righteousness. Scripture’s nonconformity goes deeper than any safety pin: "be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind" (Rom 12:2). And God has a habit of choosing the misfits: "God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise" (1Co 1:27). A father can tell his son: you want to be a rebel? Rebel against the flesh, the world, and the devil. That is the only revolution that lasts, and its King was crucified for leading it.
webster_summary: Old slang for a hoodlum or coward, reborn in 1976–77 (Ramones, Sex Pistols) as the name of fast, defiant rock and its do-it-yourself tribe; Scripture rejects anarchy (Jdg 21:25) and offers a deeper nonconformity (Rom 12:2).
webster_full: PUNK, n. and adj. (Gen X slang, 1976–77, New York and London) A fast, loud, stripped-down style of rock music; a follower of it, known by torn clothes, safety pins, and spiked or Mohawk hair; anything defiantly anti-establishment. "He’s been punk since seventh grade."
Punk rock, punk rocker, hardcore punk (early 1980s), pop punk, post-punk; the DIY ethic of self-made records and zines.
Older senses still alive: a petty hoodlum or worthless young man; a coward ("to punk out"); Elizabethan, a harlot.
Webster 1828: PUNK, n. A prostitute; a strumpet.
Decode for parents: punk often begins as a hunger for honesty; turn the rebellion against sin rather than against parents.
scriptures: In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.
There is a generation that curseth their father, and doth not bless their mother.
For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Because thou hast rejected the word of the LORD, he hath also rejected thee from being king.
Rom 12:2
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
corruption_summary: Punk made rebellion a style and anarchy a slogan; Scripture names rebellion as the sin of witchcraft and offers the only true nonconformity — a mind transformed by God.
corruption_paragraphs: Anarchy as identity. The punk slogan was that no one should rule, and the Bible has a book that shows what that looks like: Judges, where every man did what was right in his own eyes (Jdg 21:25) and the land fell apart. Rebellion against all authority is not freedom but the oldest sin in a new haircut; Samuel ranked it with witchcraft (1Sa 15:23). A movement that taught a generation to curse father and mother (Pro 30:11) left many of its children with exactly the "no future" it chanted.

What punk got right. Yet punk’s contempt for fakery, its do-it-yourself grit, and its refusal to be a consumer are not far from the kingdom. The Christian is the real nonconformist, transformed rather than conformed (Rom 12:2), and God loves to build His church out of people the respectable world wrote off — the foolish, the weak, the base (1Co 1:27). The cure for a punk is not a necktie but a cause big enough to give his life to.
roots_summary: Elizabethan punk (harlot) → American hoodlum / coward (early 1900s) → Dirty Harry (1971) → punk rock (1970s critics) → Ramones and Sex Pistols (1976–77); Scripture: be not conformed (Rom 12:2).
roots_lines: Late 16th c. punk — a harlot; origin uncertain
Early 20th c. US: a worthless young man, hoodlum, or coward; punk out
Early 1970s rock criticism: punk rock for raw garage bands
1976–77: Punk magazine, the Ramones, CBGB, the Sex Pistols; safety pins and Mohawks
Biblical nonconformity: be ye transformed (Rom 12:2); God chooses the foolish things (1Co 1:27)
usage: "You call that punk? That’s just a haircut."
Every man did that which was right in his own eyes (Jdg 21:25) — anarchy is not new.
Be not conformed to this world (Rom 12:2) — the rebellion worth joining.

etymology: Borrowed from the French Nouvelle Vague, the name for the young film-makers of the late 1950s (Truffaut, Godard). In 1976–77 the record industry adopted new wave as a friendlier label than punk for the sharper, more melodic bands coming out of the same scene — Blondie, Talking Heads, Elvis Costello, the Cars, Devo — and Sire Records’ Seymour Stein is often credited with pushing the term. In the early 1980s, carried by the new MTV, it came to mean synthesizer pop with striking hair and clothes: Duran Duran, Depeche Mode, A Flock of Seagulls ("I Ran," 1982), Tears for Fears.
biblical_def: New Wave was the music of the early MTV years: skinny ties, synthesizers, angular haircuts, and songs that sounded like the future as imagined in 1982. The name promised novelty, and every few years a fresh wave did arrive, swept the radio, and receded. The Christian observation is that waves are a good image for fashion, and the Bible uses it exactly that way. "He that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed" (Jas 1:6). Paul warns believers not to be "children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine" (Eph 4:14). The music itself is mostly harmless and often delightful; the danger is the habit it represents, of measuring everything by whether it is the newest thing. The Preacher’s word is humbling: "there is no new thing under the sun" (Ecc 1:9). The A Flock of Seagulls haircut looks as dated now as a powdered wig. And yet the Bible does not despise the new; it reserves the word for God. "Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth" (Isa 43:19). At the end of all waves stands the One who says, "Behold, I make all things new" (Rev 21:5). A father can play the old synth-pop for his kids and laugh about the hair, then teach them: trends are waves, and they go out as fast as they come in; build your life on the God whose newness never gets old.
webster_summary: Gen X music label (1976–77, from French Nouvelle Vague; early-1980s MTV synth-pop) for the melodic, stylish successor to punk; Scripture warns against being tossed by every wave (Jas 1:6) and keeps true newness for God (Rev 21:5).
webster_full: NEW WAVE, n. and adj. (Gen X slang, late 1970s–mid-1980s, US and UK) A style of rock and pop that grew out of punk, marked by synthesizers, catchy hooks, and striking fashion; also the look that went with it. "He’s gone all new wave — skinny tie and eyeliner."
From French Nouvelle Vague (late-1950s film); kin: synth-pop, post-punk, New Romantic (UK).
Icons: Blondie, Talking Heads, Devo, the Cars, Duran Duran, Depeche Mode, A Flock of Seagulls; the early-MTV video.
Webster 1828: WAVE, n. [G.] 1. A moving swell or volume of water; usually, a swell raised and driven by wind. …
Decode for parents: the music is mostly fun; the lesson is that every new wave goes back out to sea.
scriptures: Ecc 1:9
The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be; and that which is done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun.
Jas 1:6
But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed.
Eph 4:14
That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;
Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.
Rev 21:5
And he that sat upon the throne said, Behold, I make all things new. And he said unto me, Write: for these words are true and faithful.
corruption_summary: New Wave sold novelty as value, and every wave went back out; Scripture warns against being tossed by every wind and reserves true newness for the God who makes all things new.
corruption_paragraphs: Newness as a virtue. The record business learned in the late 1970s that a new label could sell old rebellion to a new crowd, and it has been naming waves ever since. A young person trained to prize the newest sound will tend to prize the newest idea, and that is how souls are carried about by every wind of doctrine (Eph 4:14). The Preacher is a sobering corrective: there is no new thing under the sun (Ecc 1:9). The truly new is rarely what the marketing calls new.

The newness that lasts. Scripture is not nostalgic; it is full of new songs, new hearts, and a new creation. But the newness comes from God, not from fashion. "Behold, I will do a new thing" (Isa 43:19) is a promise of grace, and "Behold, I make all things new" (Rev 21:5) is the last word over every passing wave. The believer can enjoy a good song from 1983 without needing it, because his hope is in a newness that never dates.
roots_summary: Old English wafian (to wave) → wave → French Nouvelle Vague film (late 1950s) → record-industry new wave (1976–77) → early-MTV synth-pop; Scripture: Behold, I make all things new (Rev 21:5).
roots_lines: Old English wafian — to wave, to move to and fro; wave of the sea
Late 1950s France: la Nouvelle Vague, the new wave of film-makers
1976–77: new wave as the record industry’s gentler name for post-punk
1981–84: MTV synth-pop — Duran Duran, Depeche Mode, A Flock of Seagulls
Biblical waves: the waverer tossed (Jas 1:6); the God who makes all things new (Rev 21:5)
usage: "Is that punk or new wave?" "It’s got a synthesizer, so it’s new wave."
He that wavereth is like a wave of the sea (Jas 1:6) — trends come and go.
Behold, I make all things new (Rev 21:5) — the only newness that lasts.

etymology: From Latin alternus, by turns, one after the other; in standard English an alternative is a choice between two or more things. In the 1980s American college radio stations and record stores used alternative for rock outside the commercial mainstream (R.E.M., The Replacements, Hüsker Dü, The Smiths); Billboard started a Modern Rock chart for it in 1988. Perry Farrell’s first Lollapalooza touring festival (1991) and Nirvana’s Nevermind the same year made alt-rock the mainstream it had defined itself against. Since the 1970s the word had also served as a euphemism ("alternative lifestyle") for what the culture once called sin.
biblical_def: In Gen X speech alternative meant music, clothes, and people outside the mainstream: college-radio bands, thrift-store style, a vague distrust of anything popular. Then the alternative became the most popular thing in America, and the word kept going anyway, as an identity rather than a description. The Christian observation is that the word assumes there is always another option, and that choosing the other option is itself a virtue. Scripture agrees that choices are real and must be made: "choose you this day whom ye will serve" (Jos 24:15). Elijah demanded that Israel stop limping between two options: "How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him" (1Ki 18:21). But the Bible does not treat the road less traveled as automatically right. Our Lord does set His way against the crowd — "wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat" (Mat 7:13) — yet the narrow way is not another style; it is a Person. "I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me" (Joh 14:6). In the one matter that counts most, there is no alternative: "Neither is there salvation in any other" (Act 4:12). The euphemism "alternative lifestyle" should be named plainly too; calling sin an alternative does not change what it is. A father can enjoy the old college-radio records with his children and teach them that being different is not the same as being right — and that the narrowest, most countercultural thing anyone can do is follow Christ.
webster_summary: Gen X label (1980s college radio; Lollapalooza and Nevermind, 1991) for rock and culture outside the mainstream; Scripture makes choice real (Jos 24:15) but admits no alternative to Christ (Act 4:12).
webster_full: ALTERNATIVE, n. and adj. (Gen X slang, 1980s–1990s, US college radio) Rock music and youth culture outside the commercial mainstream; a person who identifies with it. "She only listens to alternative."
Alt-rock, alt, modern rock, college rock; Lollapalooza (1991) its traveling showcase.
Euphemistic sense (1970s onward): alternative lifestyle, alternative family — usage that renames sin as option.
Webster 1828: ALTERNATIVE, a. Offering a choice of two things.
Decode for parents: different is not the same as right; teach the one narrow way that is not a style but a Person.
scriptures: And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
And Elijah came unto all the people, and said, How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him. And the people answered him not a word.
Mat 7:13
Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat:
Joh 14:6
Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
Act 4:12
Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
corruption_summary: Alternative makes difference a virtue and choice an identity, and lends its name to euphemisms for sin; Scripture makes the choice real and allows no alternative to Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Difference as a virtue. The alternative scene began as a reasonable distaste for corporate pop and ended as a creed: whatever the crowd likes is suspect, whatever is marginal is authentic. That creed collapsed the moment alternative became the crowd, but the habit of mind survived. A child taught that being different is good in itself will be easy prey for every new "alternative" morality. Elijah’s question cuts through it: not which option is unusual, but which God is true (1Ki 18:21).

No alternative. The world loves options because options postpone commitment. The gospel ends the shopping. Christ is the way, the truth, and the life (Joh 14:6), and there is none other name under heaven whereby we must be saved (Act 4:12). The narrow gate (Mat 7:13) is the most countercultural door in any age, and those who go through it are the real alternative — not because they are odd, but because they are His. That is a difference no record label can market and no festival can absorb.
roots_summary: Latin alternus (by turns) → English alternative (a choice) → 1970s euphemism → 1980s college-radio alternative → Lollapalooza and Nevermind (1991); Scripture: none other name (Act 4:12).
roots_lines: Latin alternus — one after the other, by turns
English alternative — a choice between two or more possibilities
1970s euphemism: alternative lifestyle
1980s college radio; 1988 Billboard Modern Rock chart; 1991 Lollapalooza and Nevermind
Biblical choice: choose you this day (Jos 24:15); no salvation in any other (Act 4:12)
usage: "They’re not punk, they’re alternative." — c. 1990.
How long halt ye between two opinions? (1Ki 18:21).
I am the way, the truth, and the life (Joh 14:6) — and there is no alternative.

etymology: A clipped form of independent (Latin in-, not, + dependere, to hang from), used of film companies outside the big studios from the early 20th century. For Gen X it meant above all the independent record labels of the late 1970s and 1980s — Rough Trade in London (1978), with Britain’s indie chart from 1980; SST, Dischord, Sub Pop, and K Records in America — and the do-it-yourself bands that toured in vans, pressed their own singles, and refused major-label money. Indie rock was a genre name by the late 1980s; indie film boomed with the Sundance festival in the early 1990s.
biblical_def: Indie was Gen X shorthand for independent: the small record label, the band that booked its own tours, the film made on a credit card. To be indie was to be untouched by corporate money, and the scene was fierce about it; signing to a major label was "selling out." The Christian observation is that half of this is admirable and half needs correcting. The admirable half is honest work and self-support. Paul himself was a kind of indie apostle, making tents so as not to lean on anyone: "Neither did we eat any man’s bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you" (2Th 3:8). He told believers to "study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands" (1Th 4:11). The do-it-yourself ethic has deep roots in the Christian work ethic. The half that needs correcting is the myth of total independence. No man is self-made. "The eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee" (1Co 12:21); we are members of a body. And before God, independence is the oldest temptation of all: "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding" (Pro 3:5). Christ puts it plainly: "without me ye can do nothing" (Joh 15:5). A father can praise his son’s homemade band and his willingness to work for every dollar, and teach him the deeper truth: the most free man alive is the one who is wholly dependent on God.
webster_summary: Gen X clipping of independent (1980s labels: Rough Trade, SST, Sub Pop) for self-made music and film outside the majors; Scripture honors the work of one’s own hands (1Th 4:11) and denies that any man is independent of God (Joh 15:5).
webster_full: INDIE, adj. and n. (Gen X slang, 1980s–1990s, UK and US) Independent of the major record labels or film studios; made on a small budget by the artists themselves; a person devoted to such music. "They were indie until the big label called."
Indie rock, indie label, indie film, indie cred; opposite: major, sellout.
The DIY ethic: self-booked tours, hand-made zines, singles pressed in the hundreds; later, indie as a look and a taste.
Webster 1828: INDEPENDENT, a. [in and dependent.] 1. Not dependent; not subject to the control of others; not subordinate. God is the only being who is perfectly independent. …
Decode for parents: honor the work ethic in it, and gently correct the myth that any of us is independent.
scriptures: Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you:
And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you;
And the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee: nor again the head to the feet, I have no need of you.
Pro 3:5
Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.
Joh 15:5
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
corruption_summary: Indie rightly honors hard, self-supporting work but feeds the myth that a man can be independent; Scripture praises the work of one’s own hands and makes every branch dependent on the Vine.
corruption_paragraphs: The myth of the self-made. Indie culture turned independence into a moral credential, and a credential easily becomes pride: the purer-than-thou contempt for anyone who sold out, the boast of needing no one. Scripture will not let any member of the body say to another, "I have no need of thee" (1Co 12:21). Before God the boast collapses entirely; to lean on our own understanding is folly (Pro 3:5), and without Christ we can do nothing (Joh 15:5).

The ethic worth keeping. Still, the indie bands that loaded their own vans and sold records out of the trunk practiced something Paul would recognize. He worked night and day so as not to be a burden (2Th 3:8), and he told Christians to work with their own hands (1Th 4:11). Self-support, thrift, and craft are Christian virtues. Teach them, and set them inside the larger truth that a man is most free when he is most dependent on the Lord.
roots_summary: Latin in- + dependere (not hanging from) → independent → indie film companies (early 1900s) → indie labels and the DIY ethic (late 1970s–80s) → indie rock; Scripture: without me ye can do nothing (Joh 15:5).
roots_lines: Latin dependere — to hang from; independent — not hanging on another
Early 20th c.: indie, a film company outside the major studios
1978–80s: Rough Trade, the UK indie chart, SST, Dischord, Sub Pop, K Records
Late 1980s indie rock; early 1990s indie film and Sundance
Biblical work and dependence: work with your own hands (1Th 4:11); abide in the Vine (Joh 15:5)
usage: "They’re on an indie label — you won’t hear them on the radio."
Work with your own hands (1Th 4:11) — the DIY ethic is older than punk.
Without me ye can do nothing (Joh 15:5) — no one is truly indie.

etymology: A plain descriptive phrase that became the name of a 1980s look: hair teased, permed, crimped, and fixed with clouds of hairspray (Aqua Net was the brand of the era) into great height and volume, with "mall bangs" rising above the forehead. Women wore it on television (Dynasty, 1981–89), on country-music stages, and in every high-school yearbook; men wore it in the "hair metal" bands of the mid-to-late 1980s (Poison, Mötley Crüe, Bon Jovi). The Texas quip "the higher the hair, the closer to God" is attached to it. The look collapsed under grunge in the early 1990s.
biblical_def: Big hair is what every Gen X yearbook photo is remembered for: teased bangs standing three inches tall, permed curls, and enough hairspray to hold it all in a stiff wind. Mothers, daughters, and long-haired rock bands all took part. The Christian observation is affectionate before it is serious. Scripture does not mock a woman’s hair; it honors it: "if a woman have long hair, it is a glory to her" (1Co 11:15). And God’s care reaches to every strand: "the very hairs of your head are all numbered" (Mat 10:30). Hair is a gift and caring for it is no sin. But the old joke — "the higher the hair, the closer to God" — gets the direction exactly backward, and Scripture says so gently. Peter writes, "Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel" (1Pe 3:3), "But let it be the hidden man of the heart… even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price" (1Pe 3:4). The point is not a ban on styling but a ranking: the heart first, the hair after. And the Bible’s own crown of hair is not volume but age: "The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness" (Pro 16:31). A father can laugh with his daughter at Mom’s 1987 prom picture, and tell her that the hair God most admires is the gray kind, earned by a long life of walking with Him.
webster_summary: Gen X name for the teased, permed, hairsprayed volume of 1980s fashion and hair-metal bands; Scripture calls a woman’s hair a glory (1Co 11:15) and ranks the hidden ornament of the heart above it (1Pe 3:4).
webster_full: BIG HAIR, n. (Gen X slang, 1980s, US) Hair styled for maximum height and volume by teasing, perming, crimping, and heavy hairspray. "Her big hair barely fit in the car."
Companions: mall bangs, teased hair, the perm, the crimping iron, Aqua Net; hair band / hair metal for its male rock form.
The Texas quip: "the higher the hair, the closer to God"; the style faded before grunge’s unwashed look after 1991.
Webster 1828: HAIR, n. 1. A small filament issuing from the skin of an animal, and from a bulbous root. …
Decode for parents: a harmless fashion with a good lesson attached — God counts every hair and still looks first at the heart.
scriptures: But if a woman have long hair, it is a glory to her: for her hair is given her for a covering.
But the very hairs of your head are all numbered.
Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness.
corruption_summary: Big hair is mostly harmless fun, but it makes height and volume the measure of beauty; Scripture honors hair as a glory and ranks the hidden ornament of the heart, and the gray head of righteousness, above it.
corruption_paragraphs: The higher the hair. The joke tied height to holiness, and it was only a joke; but the habit behind it is real. A culture that spends an hour on the bangs and no minutes on the soul has its adornment upside down. Peter does not forbid a woman to braid her hair; he forbids her to let it be her adorning (1Pe 3:3). The ornament God prizes is a meek and quiet spirit, of great price in His sight (1Pe 3:4) — and it does not wilt in the rain.

A better crown. Every big-hair photograph is now a family joke, and that is the gentle lesson of fashion: what looked glorious at the prom looks silly at the reunion. Scripture’s crown of hair does not date. The hoary head is a crown of glory when it is found in the way of righteousness (Pro 16:31), and the God who numbers every hair (Mat 10:30) loves the gray ones on the head of a faithful saint as much as the teased ones on a girl of sixteen.
roots_summary: Old English hær → hair → 1980s teased, permed, hairsprayed big hair → hair-metal bands → swept away by grunge (early 1990s); Scripture: the hoary head a crown of glory (Pro 16:31).
roots_lines: Old English hær — hair of the head or body

Television and country music: Dynasty (1981–89), the Texas quip
Mid-to-late 1980s hair metal; early 1990s grunge ends the era
Biblical hair: a glory (1Co 11:15); every hair numbered (Mat 10:30); the hoary head a crown (Pro 16:31)

Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair (1Pe 3:3).
The very hairs of your head are all numbered (Mat 10:30) — even the teased ones.
